lines.en: What the reader owes you is nothing; every sentence must earn the reading of the next.
It is not enough to be right; you must be read.
Were your strongest argument placed at the end, few readers would ever reach it.
However noble your cause, a boring opening will bury it before the second paragraph.
Not until you have written for a hostile reader have you truly written persuasively.
It is the example, not the adjective, that persuades; show the reader one family, not a thousand statistics.
What the editor deleted, to the writer's horror, were all the sentences the writer loved most.
The letter moved the minister, who read it twice, and then, to everyone's astonishment, acted on it.
Little persuades so quietly as admitting the strength of the other side before you answer it.
Rarely does shouting convince the reader; the quiet, well-built sentence does.
What the writer cut in the fifth draft was everything the first draft had been so proud of.
It is the verb, not the adverb, that carries the weight; 'she sprinted' beats 'she ran very quickly'.
Were every sentence forced to justify its place, most pages would shrink by half and improve by double.
Not until the statistics were replaced by one woman's name did the readers begin to care.
However strong your evidence, present it as a lecture and the reader will defend the opposite view.
